beginner: Oil prices are spiking because of the war with Iran, pushing gasoline up 18.9% and inflation to 3.3% in March. This is the highest inflation has been in nearly two years.
The Federal Reserve cannot cut interest rates right now because energy costs keep pushing prices higher. Rate cuts have to wait until the energy shock fades.
The economy is still growing steadily at 2.4%, so the Fed does not need to panic. The real test is whether inflation comes back down when oil prices stabilize.
moderate: March's 3.3% inflation print arrived on the back of 12.5% energy cost increases, reversing the disinflationary trend of late 2025. Energy-driven shocks are temporary by nature, but they matter for Fed policy timing in the near term.

The Fed signaled it has little room to cut rates this year because upside risks to inflation remain elevated. Compare this to February's 2.41% CPI reading, which suggested disinflationary momentum was building, and you see how quickly the calculus shifted.

Underlying growth at 2.4% remains solid enough to absorb a temporary inflation spike. The risk is if energy prices stay elevated longer than expected, or if inflation psychology shifts and consumers demand higher wage growth.
expert: CPI jumped 90 basis points month-over-month (February 2.41% to March 3.3%), with energy accounting for roughly two-thirds of the move. The war shock is real and pushes the terminal rate higher than the 3.25% forecast full-year level.

Core PCE (the Fed's preferred gauge) is forecast to fall back to 2% in H1 2027, suggesting policymakers expect the energy shock to be transitory. The market is pricing in no rate cuts until Q3 2026 at the earliest.

Watch the weekly Petroleum Status Report and crude futures for signals on whether energy costs stabilize. If Brent holds above $95/bbl through Q2, the Fed may need to guide forward expectations higher for the terminal rate.

beginner: Canada's inflation is running at 1.78%, well below the Bank of Canada's 2% target, giving the central bank room to cut rates if the economy weakens.
Trade tensions with the US are putting pressure on Canadian businesses and holding back investment. This matters because Canada relies on cross-border trade to grow.
Unemployment at 6.74% is elevated compared to the US, suggesting Canada's labor market is weaker. The Bank of Canada will likely need to support growth with lower rates this year.
moderate: February's 1.78% CPI reading is significantly below the 2% full-year forecast, and trade friction with the US is pushing business confidence lower. This creates room for the BoC to cut rates, but only if growth remains weak.

Unemployment at 6.74% in January was the highest in over a decade relative to historical Canadian norms, reflecting broader North American trade uncertainty. The policy rate at 2.25% is already the lowest in this cycle, so the BoC has limited dry powder left.

The current account is expected to stay near balance (negative 0.5% of GDP), but trade tension could worsen the external position. Watch for business investment surveys in Q2 to gauge whether tariff uncertainty is causing firms to delay projects.
expert: CPI at 1.78% against a 2% full-year forecast suggests disinflation is tracking faster than expected, likely driven by subdued domestic demand and energy price normalization. Core inflation is likely even softer.
The BoC has cut rates to 2.25%, below the neutral rate estimate of 2.5-3%, and markets price in 75-100 bps of additional cuts by year-end. Trade uncertainty is the binding constraint, not inflation.

Monitor Q1 GDP (due late May) and business investment intentions surveys. If investment drops more than 5% year-over-year, expect accelerated BoC easing in June. Watch the CAD/USD cross for signs of capital flight.

beginner: UK consumer confidence just crashed to 43.30 in April, the lowest reading in months. Consumers are worried about their wallets and cutting back spending.

The government has very little room to spend money to help the economy because the budget deficit is already large. This means the central bank cannot count on fiscal stimulus to offset higher energy prices.

The UK economy is growing slowly at 1.5% forecast for the year, and weak investment and productivity are holding it back. Without support from either fiscal or monetary policy, growth could disappoint.
moderate: Consumer confidence fell to 43.30 from 46 in April, tracking the highest CPI reading since early 2022 at 3.24% in February. Energy prices and cost-of-living anxiety are weighing on households faster than economists expected.

The Budget Deficit at 4% of GDP leaves little fiscal space to cushion an inflation shock, and the Bank of England's policy rate at 3.75% is already restrictive. The UK faces a squeeze between inflation from energy imports and the inability to use policy tools to offset it.

Private sector investment remains weak despite a stable 3.75% policy rate, suggesting business confidence is cracking under cost pressures and demand uncertainty. This creates a risk that growth undershoots the 1.5% forecast if consumers pull back further.
expert: CPI at 3.24% in February is tracking above the 2.5% full-year forecast on energy and import costs, while consumer confidence at 43.3 signals demand destruction is beginning. The BoE faces stagflationary pressure without policy relief from the Treasury.

The fiscal-monetary policy mix is constraining: the 4% budget deficit precludes expansionary stimulus, and a 3.75% policy rate is contractionary in real terms if energy inflation persists. Forward guidance from the MPC suggests rates will stay elevated longer than initially priced.

Watch April and May PMI prints (due early May and early June) for signs of demand contraction. If manufacturing PMI breaks below 50 while services PMI stays above 52, expect the BoE to cut rates in Q3 despite lingering inflation.

beginner: Japanese workers got a 3.3% pay raise in February, blowing past expectations. This gives the Bank of Japan confidence to keep raising interest rates and gradually tightening policy.
But consumer confidence just crashed to 33.3 in April, the worst level since the pandemic hit. Households are worried even though wages are rising, which is unusual and concerning.
The yen is weak and energy prices are climbing, pushing producer costs up 2.6%. A weak currency makes imports expensive, and that could start showing up in consumer prices soon.
moderate: Cash earnings surged 3.3% year-over-year in February, well above the 2.7% consensus and above nominal wage growth rates seen since 2019. This gives the BoJ political cover to continue rate normalization toward the 1.25% full-year forecast level.

Consumer confidence crashed to 33.3 in April despite rising wages, signaling that households are more worried about future purchasing power than current income gains. This disconnect suggests they expect inflation or job losses ahead.

Producer prices at 2.6% and yen weakness from Bank of Japan rate hiking are creating a pass-through risk to CPI. The 1.26% CPI print in February masks imported inflation that may accelerate in coming months.
expert: Real wage growth at 3.3% nominal minus 1.26% CPI yields approximately 2% real wage gains, the strongest in years, giving the BoJ justification for the 0.75% policy rate in February and signaling further hikes toward 1.25% by year-end.

Consumer confidence at 33.3 represents a 19-point collapse from pre-pandemic levels despite wage gains, suggesting households are discounting future purchasing power. Core inflation expectations are likely unanchoring from the 2% target.

Monitor April CPI (due mid-May) and the next BoJ rate decision (late April) for forward guidance on terminal rate. If inflation expectations in household surveys breach 2.5% despite still-soft CPI, expect the BoJ to accelerate normalization beyond 1.25%.

beginner: German factories are still shrinking, not growing. Industrial output fell short of expectations in February, meaning the recession that started last year is dragging on longer than anyone hoped.
Germans are losing confidence in their economy fast. Consumer sentiment crashed from 44.73 to 41.80 in April, matching a broader European panic about jobs and spending power.

Germany's reliance on imported energy is a structural vulnerability. When energy prices spike (whether from war, weather, or supply shocks), German growth gets punched because manufacturing cannot absorb the cost shock easily.
moderate: Industrial production fell 0.3% month-on-month in February versus 0.6% consensus, extending a recession that has now lasted longer than the 2008 financial crisis downturn. This is not a temporary soft patch anymore.

Consumer confidence plunged to 41.80 from 42.03 in April, part of a synchronized collapse across the eurozone. Germany's own survey shows worse sentiment than Italy and France, despite lower unemployment at 3.6%, suggesting households are pricing in persistent weakness ahead.

Germany's current account surplus of 4.5% GDP masks a fragile domestic story. Export dependence and energy import vulnerability mean the economy has no shock absorber when external demand weakens or geopolitical risk raises input costs.
expert: Industrial production missed consensus by 0.3 points in February, confirming the industrial recession is not reverting to trend. With policy rates holding at 2.15% versus a 2.5% forecast year-end, the ECB faces a growth collapse risk if it raises further.

Consumer confidence at 41.80 versus Italy's 43.12 and France's 38.08 reveals Germany's confidence loss is driven by manufacturing sector weakness, not aggregate demand shock. Unemployment at 3.6% should support consumption, but it is not, signaling household expectations have turned negative on income durability.

Watch for a fiscal pivot. A 2% budget deficit forecast and 4.5% current account surplus give Berlin room to spend, but political consensus around deficit discipline may fracture if Q2 growth data disappoints further, forcing a structural policy choice between austerity and stimulus.

beginner: France's economy is slowing down. Growth is expected to creep along at 0.7% this year, held up mostly by factories rebuilding inventory after running down stock, not by real demand.

French consumers are also pulling back. Confidence dropped from 42.03 to 38.08 in April, the lowest of the three major eurozone economies shown here, signaling households are worried about their wallets.
France faces a structural employment problem. Unemployment sits at 7.7%, nearly double Germany's 3.6%, which limits how much French households can spend even if confidence stabilizes.
moderate: French growth at 0.7% in 2025 is hollow because it relies on aeronautics inventory rebuilding, not underlying demand. Once factories finish restocking, growth will drop further unless consumption revives, which 0.9% 2026 growth barely signals.

Consumer confidence crashed to 38.08 from 42.03, the steepest decline of the three major eurozone countries, despite inflation at 0.9% (lowest among peers). The problem is not price shocks but weak labor market prospects given 7.7% unemployment.

France's budget deficit at 4.8% GDP is the highest of the three eurozone countries, leaving little fiscal flexibility to support demand if growth disappoints further. The ECB's 2.15% policy rate gives room to cut, but France needs structural reform in labor markets, not just monetary relief.
expert: French GDP growth at 0.7% in 2025 is inventory-driven with limited top-line demand signal. The 2026 forecast of 0.9% growth suggests only modest momentum pickup despite a 1.4% full-year consensus, and CPI at 0.9% in February (versus 2% forecast) confirms deflationary bias persists.

Consumer confidence at 38.08 represents the worst mood among the three major eurozone economies despite France's lower inflation environment. Unemployment at 7.7% explains it: the labor market is not tight enough to drive wage growth or spending confidence, and inventory-led growth does not create persistent jobs.

France's 4.8% budget deficit leaves limited room for fiscal maneuver if Q2 data confirms stalled consumption. Watch whether the ECB accelerates rate cuts beyond current 2.15% policy rate, as France's political room for fiscal tightening (required under EU rules) may not exist if growth continues to disappoint.

beginner: Italy is the bright spot in Europe right now. It showed stronger growth momentum than Germany or France earlier this year, suggesting Italian households and businesses are still spending.
But Italian consumer confidence is still falling. Sentiment dropped from 47.53 to 43.12 in April, which means even Italy's relative strength may not last if households get spooked.

Italy's borrowing costs are rising. Government bond yields jumped from 2.372% to 2.604%, which means the government will pay more to borrow money. This pushes back against lower borrowing costs that would normally help growth accelerate.
moderate: Italy showed stronger growth momentum earlier in the year than both Germany and France, but consumer confidence dropped from 47.53 to 43.12 in April, erasing the sentiment advantage. The gap between economic activity and household mood suggests forward growth risk.

Italian 12-month BOT yields cleared at 2.604% versus 2.372% prior, up 23 basis points, while ECB policy rates hold at 2.15%. Rising yields on government debt signal markets are repricing Italy risk (fiscal sustainability concerns or eurozone fragmentation fears), not falling real rates supporting growth.

Italy's unemployment at 5.6% is better than France's 7.7% but still higher than Germany's 3.6%, limiting wage pressures that would lift consumption. Inflation at 1.51% in February is the lowest of the three, confirming demand weakness is the constraint, not price shocks.
expert: Italy's stronger growth momentum in early 2026 contrasts with Germany and France weakness, but consumer confidence at 43.12 (highest of the three but still declining from 47.53) signals the advantage is not durable without sustained labor market tightening.

12-month BOT yields at 2.604% versus 2.372% prior (up 23 basis points) while ECB policy rate holds at 2.15% shows real yields are rising, not falling. This reprices Italy fiscal risk or eurozone tail risk, both of which would choke investment and consumption if widening spreads persist.

Watch Italy's 1% current account surplus and 5.6% unemployment. If rising borrowing costs force fiscal tightening (budget deficit forecast at 3.2% GDP), Italy risks a growth-killing policy shock that could trigger a broader eurozone fragmentation trade if bond spreads widen further.

beginner: China is losing money fast. Foreign reserves dropped by $86 billion, the biggest decline among Asian countries, draining war-related resources and showing China is burning through cash.
But China's economy is starting to stabilize. Exports are leading the recovery, and domestic spending is picking up too, suggesting the worst slowdown may be behind us.

Deflation is still a problem for China. Prices barely rose in January (0.23% CPI), which means households and businesses have no inflation relief and keep delaying purchases, betting prices will fall further.
moderate: Foreign reserves fell $86 billion, the clearest casualty of the war among Asian economies and the lowest reserves level since mid-2024. At this burn rate, China's buffer is eroding faster than GDP growth can replace it, forcing difficult choices about capital controls or reserve depletion.

GDP growth is stabilizing with exports leading but domestic consumption picking up. This two-speed recovery (external demand plus consumer bounce) is more durable than pure export-led growth, but relies on consumers not fearing further deflation or unemployment spikes.

Deflation at 0.23% CPI in January despite the war indicates a structural demand problem, not a temporary supply shock. China's 4.5% GDP growth forecast for 2026 assumes this demand weakness reverses on its own, but deflation typically requires policy stimulus to break, and China's fiscal deficit at 6.8% GDP is already high.
expert: Foreign reserves fell $86 billion month-on-month (largest declines since mid-2024), signaling capital outflows and war-related resource depletion accelerating. At current burn rate, China's reserve buffer shrinks 15-20% annually versus nominal GDP growth of 4-5%, forcing eventual policy tightening or RMB depreciation.

China's economic stabilization shows exports rebounding and consumption picking up, but CPI at 0.23% (versus 2% forecast) confirms persistent deflation despite war supply shocks. This reflects demand weakness deeper than supply constraints, meaning consumer spending gains may be temporary if households expect further disinflation.

Watch China's 2.75% policy rate versus 2.5% full-year forecast. If reserves continue falling and RMB depreciation pressures mount, the PBOC may need to hike rates defensively before cutting again, which would choke domestic demand recovery and trigger a harder landing than the 4.7% GDP forecast implies.

beginner: India's growth engine is firing, but it runs on imported oil. When global energy prices spike, the rupee weakens and stock prices fall, cutting into the wealth that fuels consumer spending.
Consumer confidence just jumped from 57 to 66 because the central bank held rates steady and people believe in domestic strength. This mood matters more than any single inflation number right now.
The real vulnerability is external. Energy dependence means India stays hostage to global oil shocks, even as domestic inflation stays tame at 1.3%.
moderate: Consumer confidence surged to 66 from 57 on RBI policy hold and domestic resilience, but this optimism masks a critical dependency. India imports energy and stays vulnerable to price spikes, which already show up in rupee depreciation and falling equities. Compare this to 2023, when similar external shocks triggered far sharper currency moves because reserves were lower.

At 1.3%, December CPI looks like a central bank win, but inflation expectations are anchored by low oil prices, not by policy credibility alone. When crude inevitably rises again, the RBI will face a choice between defending the rupee and defending growth. The 5.25% policy rate leaves room to move, but not much.

Fiscal discipline and low unemployment at 4.2% support the 7.5% to 7.8% growth forecast, but the current account deficit sits at 1.2% of GDP and energy import bills are rising. Watch whether the April trade data shows goods exports holding up or cracking under external demand weakness.
expert: CPI at 1.33% in December and policy rate at 5.25% in January signal the RBI is ahead of the inflation curve, but rupee depreciation and equity weakness reflect external vulnerability. The surge in consumer confidence from 57.26 to 66.17 is real, but it rides on a commodity price floor that history says won't hold.

Current account deficit at 1.2% of GDP plus energy import exposure creates a directional risk. If crude exceeds $90/bbl sustained, the RBI faces a Phillips curve dilemma: defend the currency through rate hikes and sacrifice the 7.5% to 7.8% growth forecast, or let the rupee weaken and import inflation. The policy rate at 5.25% is not restrictive enough to anchor expectations if global oil moves sharply higher.

Leading indicator: watch March trade data and April forex flows. If energy import bills sustain above trend and FX reserves show stress, the RBI will signal a rate hike in the April 9 MPC review despite strong domestic confidence. That move would be a 150 to 200 basis point repricing from current market expectations.

beginner: South Africa burned through $3.3 billion in foreign reserves just to stop the currency from collapsing. That is not a sign of strength, it is a sign the central bank is fighting a losing battle against external shocks.
Manufacturing fell 2.2% in one month and 2.8% over the year. This is not a soft landing, this is the economy losing momentum fast.
The PMI barely stayed above 50, meaning the factory sector is on life support. One more shock and it flips into contraction.
moderate: SARB burned $3.3 billion in FX reserves to defend the rand against the oil shock, but manufacturing fell 2.8% year-on-year, a sharp reversal from prior growth. The PMI at 50.8 is not expansion, it is the line between contraction and survival. Compare this to Brazil, which benefits from higher oil as a net exporter, while South Africa bleeds reserves.

CPI at 2.96% in February looks benign, but it masks the real problem: unemployment at 31.88% means the central bank cannot cut rates without risking currency flight, and cannot hold rates without crushing demand. The policy rate at 6.75% is doing nothing to support growth because it is fighting a currency war it is losing.

The 1.5% growth forecast for 2026 assumes no further external shocks. Watch the rand weakness and FX reserve trends. If reserves fall below $75 billion or the rand breaks through 18 per USD, the SARB will have to choose between defending the currency through emergency rate hikes or allowing inflation pass-through. Either path kills growth.
expert: FX reserves at $77.76 billion down $3.3 billion month-on-month, manufacturing PMI at 50.8, and factory output at minus 2.8% year-on-year signal a country under external stress. The rand is being tested, SARB is intervening, and the real sector is rolling over. CPI at 2.96% and policy rate at 6.75% are not tight enough to stop currency depreciation but are tight enough to throttle demand.

The directional signal is deterioration. February manufacturing fell 2.2% month-on-month, the PMI is barely in expansion, and FX reserves are being drawn down. If the rand breaks 18 per USD and reserves fall below $75 billion, the SARB will face a binary choice: emergency rate hikes to 8%+ (crushing the 1.5% growth forecast) or acceptance of rand weakness and imported inflation pass-through (triggering a wage-price spiral given 31.88% unemployment).

Forward implication: watch March manufacturing PMI and April FX reserve prints. If reserves fall to $74 billion or below while the rand weakens through 18.5, expect an emergency SARB communication signaling rate hikes ahead of the May 29 MPC decision. The 1.5% growth forecast becomes obsolete and 2026 becomes a defensive scenario where negative real rates and currency weakness drive capital flight.

beginner: Brazil's trade surplus fell short of expectations in March because energy imports are eating the profits from higher oil prices. Brazil is supposed to be winning from expensive oil, but it is losing anyway.
Consumer confidence crashed to 49 because people are terrified of inflation. The central bank is charging 15% to borrow money, and families are pulling back.
Rising energy costs plus weak consumer demand is a trap. Exports slow, inflation persists, and the central bank has to keep rates sky-high.
moderate: March trade surplus at $6.41 billion missed consensus at $7.40 billion, not because exports fell but because energy imports surged. Brazil is a net energy exporter, so higher crude should help, but global crude is being disrupted and Brazil's import bill is rising faster than export revenues. Consumer confidence at 49.22 reflects the reality: the central bank's 15% policy rate is destroying household demand and the Copom faces a credibility crisis.

CPI at 3.81% in February sits inside the target band, but it is rising. The central bank held the policy rate at 15% in February and has not cut since December, signaling no relief coming. Compare this to India, which can afford to wait for inflation to fall because external shocks are managed. Brazil cannot wait because every month of 15% rates crushes growth and consumer confidence further.

The April 28-29 Copom decision is the fulcrum. Inflation expectations are drifting, unemployment is low at 5.8%, and the real effective exchange rate is depreciating. If Copom cuts 50 basis points, it signals confidence inflation will stabilize and the currency can weaken in a controlled manner. If it holds or hikes, growth for 2026 undershoots the 1.7% forecast and capital flows out.
expert: Trade surplus at $6.41 billion versus $7.40 billion consensus reflects rising energy import costs offsetting export strength. CPI at 3.81%, policy rate at 15%, and consumer confidence at 49.22 signal a central bank trapped between inflation expectations drift and demand destruction. The Copom has not cut since December and the market prices two cuts this year against a backdrop of sticky core inflation.

Directional signal: the 15% policy rate is unsustainable politically and economically, but cutting into 3.81% inflation with rising energy costs is a gamble. The April 28-29 Copom decision will reveal whether the central bank believes inflation is anchored or slipping. A 50 basis point cut signals confidence; a hold signals panic about pass-through from energy and currency weakness.

Forward implication: if energy import costs stay elevated and Copom cuts in April, the real effective exchange rate will weaken further, imported inflation accelerates, and the central bank faces a second-half repricing of terminal rate expectations. If Copom holds at 15%, the 1.7% growth forecast is at risk and capital flight accelerates. Watch March CPI print (due April 11) and the April 28 Copom decision. A 50 basis point cut plus stable inflation expectations would stabilize the outlook; a hold at 15% means the 2026 growth forecast falls to 1.0% or lower.

beginner: Higher oil prices could boost Russia's economy, but they would also give the Kremlin more cash to fund the war in Ukraine. This is not good for Russia's neighbors or for global stability.
Russia's growth is expected to slow to 0.8% next year because of sanctions, not because of oil prices. The economy is grinding down under the weight of military spending and isolation.
CPI at 6% and policy rate at 15.5% show inflation is real and the central bank is fighting hard. But this tightness will not fix the structural damage from war and sanctions.
moderate: Rising oil prices offer Russia a temporary windfall, but the Kremlin will spend it on the war in Ukraine, not on investment or growth. The forecast of 0.8% growth in 2026 reflects this reality: sanctions, capital flight, and military spending drain the economy faster than higher oil revenues can help. CPI at 6.01% and policy rate at 15.5% signal the central bank is fighting inflation but losing, because the ruble is weak and import costs are rising.

Unemployment at 2.15% looks tight, but it reflects military conscription and emigration, not strength. The policy rate at 15.5% is the highest in the dataset and signals desperation, not confidence. Compare this to Brazil's 15%: Brazil is fighting inflation in a market economy with functioning institutions. Russia is using rates as a war finance tool.

Watch energy prices and capital outflows. If crude sustains above $75 and Russia captures the windfall, it extends the war timeline and the pain for neighbors. If crude falls or Russia faces new sanctions on energy, the 0.8% growth forecast is too optimistic and the economy contracts. Either way, Russia's isolation deepens.
expert: CPI at 6.01% in January and policy rate at 15.5% in February mask a fundamental problem: the ruble is depreciating, capital is fleeing, and the central bank is rationing credit to prop up the military-industrial complex. The 2.15% unemployment rate reflects conscription and emigration, not labor market tightness. Oil prices at $75-80/bbl provide a cash windfall that the Kremlin will deploy to the war, not to productive investment.

Directional signal: growth is decelerating structurally. The 0.8% forecast for 2026 assumes some stabilization in demand and capital controls holding. If new US or EU sanctions target energy (the 40% of government revenue), or if capital outflows accelerate, growth turns negative. The policy rate at 15.5% is already at war-time levels and cannot go much higher without inducing a credit crunch.

Forward implication: watch crude prices and US sanctions announcements. If crude stays above $80 and new sanctions are delayed, Russia muddles through 2026 with near-zero growth, high inflation, and steady capital flight. If sanctions target energy exports or target the central bank directly, the ruble crashes, inflation spikes above 10%, and the 0.8% forecast becomes minus 2%. The war timeline is now pegged to oil prices and geopolitical risk, not to economic fundamentals.
